title: Rabbi Yonah (Father of Rabbi Mani)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Rabbi Yonah. (The father of Rabbi Mani.)

Hyman writes: This great Amora, who filled the Jerusalem Talmud with his halakhot and was among the heads of the generation in the fourth generation, still had the privilege of receiving from the father of the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Yochanan, as in [Bekhorot 30a:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.30a.13): “Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yirmeyah were students of Rabbi Ze’iri — and some say Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Zeira were students of Rabbi Yochanan.” The doubt is the Talmud’s, for in truth Rabbi Yonah received his Torah from the students of Rabbi Yochanan, since he was then young while Rabbi Yochanan was already very old; but he still merited to be called also Rabbi Yochanan’s student, like Rabbi Zeira. So it is in [Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 1:1:25](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yoma.1.1.25): “Rabbi Yirmeyah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: And the holy garments … Rabbi Yonah said to him: I was with you, and (Rabbi Yochanan) did not say ‘serves’ but ‘is consulted.’”

Likewise [Bava Metzia 57a:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.57a.2): “Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yirmeyah both said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name”; and in [Jerusalem Talmud Challah 1:1:14](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Challah.1.1.14): “Rabbi Yonah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.” Hyman argues that in truth both were young and merited to receive from Rabbi Yochanan only at the end of his days, and they were distinguished students of Rabbi Yochanan’s students; only Rabbi Yirmeyah grew and prospered, as explained in his entry.
Likewise we find Rabbi Yonah in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in Berakhot 3:1 and 3:5, Terumot 4:2 and Challah 1:3.

But his distinguished teachers were Rabbi Ila, as stated explicitly in Terumot 2:4: “Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose both say … Rabbi Acha said to them: So Rabbi Ila your teacher held it.” In [Avodah Zarah 13b:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.13b.6) Rabbi Yonah found Rabbi Ilai (Hyman says it should read Ila’i, according to Dikdukei Soferim) and asked him; and in Yevamot 1:2 he spoke in Rabbi Ila’s name.

Likewise Rabbi Zeira (in the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Ze’ira) was his distinguished teacher, as in [Bekhorot 30a:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.30a.13): “Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yirmeyah were students of Rabbi Ze’iri”; “Rabbi Yonah said in the name of Rabbi Zeira,” as in [Berakhot 14a:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.14a.15), [Gittin 59a:18](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.59a.18), [Avodah Zarah 14a:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.14a.6) and [Jerusalem Talmud Challah 3:5:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Challah.3.5.7). Likewise [Chullin 43b:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.43b.11), “Yonah said in the name of Zeira” — Dikdukei Soferim’s reading from the Rif, Constantinople printing, is “Rabbi Yonah said in the name of Rabbi Zeira”; and in Megillah 15b, according to the reading of the Rif and Ein Yaakov, he asked before Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbi Zeira was angry with him, as in [Jerusalem Talmud Orlah 3:1:16](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Orlah.3.1.16).[^15]

Hyman writes: Likewise Rabbi Yirmeyah — although he himself was Rabbi Zeira’s student, he was older than Rabbi Yonah, and Rabbi Yonah received from him, as in [Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:5:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Megillah.4.5.3): Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yosah went up to pay a visit to the brother of Yehudah bar Tamuzah, a relative of Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, in the synagogue of Sugna; Rabbi Yirmeyah was there and objected. Rabbi Yonah said to Rabbi Yosah, “Do they compel?” Rabbi Yosah replied, “But your teacher (Rabbi Yirmeyah) objects.” Likewise [Jerusalem Talmud Challah 1:1:22](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Challah.1.1.22): “Rabbi Yonah said: The objection was raised before Rabbi Yirmeyah.” There, 2:1, he asked before Rabbi Yirmeyah.
Now besides these teachers he had traditions from all the great men of the generation and spoke in their names.
He spoke in the name of Rabbi Abba, as in Berakhot 4:1 and Kiddushin 4:7; he asked Rabbi Abba, as in Kilayim 9:3 and Taanit 4:1, folio 15b.
In the name of Rabbi Abba bar Mamal, as in Sukkah, beginning of chapter 5.
In the name of Rabbi Abbahu, as at the end of Maaserot, chapter 5, Challah 1:5 and the end of Megillah, chapter 1.
In the name of Rabbi Ami, as in Terumot 4:5.
In the name of Rabbi Acha, as in Berakhot 2:4, folio 15b.
In the name of Rabbi Ami, as in [Chagigah 24b:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.24b.3) and Challah 1:1, folio 20b.
In the name of Rabbi Hoshaya, as in Maaser Sheni 2:1.
In the name of Rav Hamnuna, as in Maaserot 4:2 and Yevamot 8:6.
In the name of Rabbi Chiyyah (Rabbi Huna), as in Pesachim, beginning of chapter 8.

Rabbi Chaggai, as in [Rosh Hashanah 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Rosh_Hashanah.2.5.2): Hyman cites the example of Rabbi Chaggai opening the discussion and Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose concluding it.[^13]
In the name of Chizkiyah, as in Challah, beginning of halakhah 1 of chapter 1.
In the name of Rabbi Chiyya [bar Abba], as in Challah, chapter 2, end of halakhah 2, and beginning of chapter 3, the beginning of Kilayim, the end of Bikkurim, and Chagigah 3:1.
In the name of Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina, as in [Bereshit Rabbah 48:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.48.12).
In the name of Rabbi Chama bar Ukva, as in Eruvin 3:6.
In the name of Rabbi Chananyah, colleague of the Rabbis, as in Challah 4:4; he asked him, [Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 3:5:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.5.13).
In the name of Rav Chisda, as in Berakhot 2:4.
In the name of Rabbi Yose ben Gezirah, in the Jerusalem Talmud, end of Berakhot.
In the name of Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Chanina, as in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 3:1, the end of Kilayim, chapter 3, and Nazir 7:1.
In the name of Rabbi Yannai, as in Terumot 5:2.
In the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachman, as in Rosh Hashanah, beginning of chapter 1.
In the name of Rabbi Meyasha, as in Bikkurim 2:5.
In the name of Rav Nachman bar Ada, as in Berakhot 2:5.
In the name of Rav Nachman bar Yaakov or Mar Ukvan, as in Eruvin 6:1: “Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose — one in the name of Mar Ukvan and one in the name of Rav Nachman bar Yaakov.”
In the name of Ulla bar Yishmael, as in Kilayim, beginning of chapter 9.
In the name of Rabbi Krispa, in the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Ketubot.
In the name of Bar Kappara, in the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Yoma.
In the name of Rav, as in Berakhot 4:3.
In the name of Shmuel, as in Challah, beginning of halakhah 1 of chapter 1, and Kiddushin, beginning of chapter 1.
In the name of Rabbi Shmuel of Cappadocia. Hyman cites the end of halakhah 1 with a chapter number outside the standard division of Challah. A parallel is in Jerusalem Talmud Challah 3:1.

In the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, as in Taanit 3:9; Hyman considers this saying to have become corrupted at the end of Vayikra Rabbah, chapter 34, where it reads Rabbi Yonah bar Abba; he says it should read “in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Abba.”
In the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Zekharyah, as in Demai 2:1.
In the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida, as in Maaserot 1:2 and Berakhot, chapter 6, end of halakhah 1.
In the name of Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiyya, as in Berakhot 5:1.

Hyman thinks that apparently after Rabbi Ami’s death no further head of the academy was established, but there were fixed gatherings of sages in several places, and they were called “the Rabbis of Caesarea”; they likewise spread Torah in Tzippori. Then Rabbi Yonah, with his colleague and beloved Rabbi Yose, spread much Torah in Tiberias with many students, as in [Sanhedrin 1:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sanhedrin.1.2.11), where they said, “Rabbi Chaggai opened; Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose concluded.” Hyman says that Rabbi Chaggai was in Tiberias, citing [Moed Katan 25a:19-21](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.25a.19-21), and that the sage designated ר״ח is buried there.[^9]

In Sheviit, chapter 3, end of halakhah 1, Rabbi Yonah said … they said to him, “But they are with you in Tiberias”; but Hyman finds little proof in that passage, for possibly a scribal error fell in there, and the source is Tosefta Sheviit, beginning of chapter 4, where they said to Rabbi Yehudah, “But they are with you in Tiberias.” Hyman writes that we always find these two colleagues together, as in Sheviit 4:2, where Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose permitted baking bread on Shabbat for the soldiers; and in Berakhot 6:5 both went up to the feast of Rabbi Chanana Antanaya.

Likewise they are mentioned together in Berakhot 3:1 and 3:4, Terumot 2:4 and Eruvin 6:1. Both went up to pay a visit to the brother of Yehudah ben Tamuzah, as in [Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:5:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Megillah.4.5.3). In Berakhot 5:1 it is related that both came to Antioch, and Ursicinus (the city governor) saw them and rose before them, and said that he had seen their likeness in battle and through this was victorious. Likewise both were partners in wine, as in [Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni 4:6:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Maaser_Sheni.4.6.4). Their disputes we find in several places in the Jerusalem Talmud and also in the Babylonian Talmud, as in [Menachot 70b:12-15](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.70b.12-15), where Rabbi Yose bar Zavda (whom Hyman identifies as Rabbi Yose of the Jerusalem Talmud without further designation) disagrees with Rabbi Yonah. In Nedarim 9:1: when Rabbi Yose’s son died and the news came to Rabbi Yonah, who was then in Tyre, he completed the whole day in fasting.
Likewise we find Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose the Galilean together, as in Berakhot, chapter 3, end of halakhah 1.

Hyman argues that although Rabbi Yonah was not head of the academy, he had a great academy and many students before him, as we find that Rabbi Inyanya bar Sasai went up to Rabbi Yonah’s house, as in Maaser Sheni, chapter 4, end of halakhah 3.
Rabbi Elazar bar Merom raised an objection before him, as in Taanit 4:3.
Rabbi Ashyan in his name, as in Terumot, beginning of chapter 1.
Rabbi Gurion was younger than Rabbi Yonah, as in [Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 3:5:19](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.5.19).
Rabbi Zavdi son of Rabbi Yaakov bar Zavdi in his name, as in Berakhot 1:2, folio 6b.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Maryah asked before him, as in Ketubot 9:1.
Rabbi Yudan bar Palai raised an objection before him, as at the beginning of Sheviit, chapter 5 (there bar Padya, which Hyman considers an error).
Rabbi Yehoshua of the South before him, as at the end of Sukkah, chapter 4.
Rabbi Yose of the South before him, as in Shevuot 1:8.
Rabbi Yitzchak, son of Rabbi Chiyya, in Rabbi Yonah’s name, as in [Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 12:4:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yevamot.12.4.5).
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ketzutzta in his name, as in Rosh Hashanah, beginning of halakhah 1 of chapter 1.
Rabbi Leontei in his name, as in Demai 7:7; he asked him, Yevamot 9:8; he bathed with him, Shabbat 3:3.

Rabbi Nicha bar Saba asked before him, as at the beginning of Yevamot, chapter 9. In [Eruvin, chapter 2, end of halakhah 1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Eruvin.2.1.9), Rabbi Yonah reports that Rabbi Nasa asked whether one may carry between the posts, and at [the beginning of Bava Metzia, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Bava_Metzia.3.1.2), Rabbi Nasa transmits a teaching in Rabbi Yonah’s name; Hyman infers from this that they were like colleagues.
Rabbi Philippa bar Peruta spoke before him, as in Megillah, chapter 1, end of halakhah 1, and Soferim 21:7. Rabbi Pinchas the chaver in his name, as in Shemot Rabbah 1:14.
Rabbi Redifa in his name, as in Pesachim, beginning of chapter 8, and Yevamot 1:2.
Hyman writes that he was so great that his name was heard in Babylonia, as in [Zevachim 107a:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.107a.1), where Rava speaks in accordance with Rabbi Yonah, etc.

Rabbi Yonah was called one of “the forceful ones of the Land of Israel,” as in [Taanit 23b:9-10](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.23b.9-10), where Rabbi Zerika said to Rav Safra: “Come and see the difference between the forceful ones of the Land of Israel and the pious ones of Babylonia. The pious ones of Babylonia — Rav Huna and Rav Chisda … the forceful ones of the Land of Israel — such as Rabbi Yonah, the father of Rabbi Mani: when the world needed rain … he prayed for mercy and rain came, and even his household did not know that the rain came because of him.” Hyman thinks he was called so because he said to Rabbi Gurion, [Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 3:5:19](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.5.19), “We do not learn from a person of lesser standing.” In Yoma 8:5 and Nedarim 4:9: once a fire broke out in his neighborhood, and a gentile wanted to extinguish it, and he did not let him (for it was Shabbat); a miracle occurred and the whole neighborhood was saved. His love for the Torah was so great that they said in Maaser Sheni 5:3 that he gave his tithe to Rabbi Acha bar Ulla, not because he was a Kohen but because he labored in Torah. In [Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 4:1:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.4.1.6): when he prayed in the synagogue he prayed silently, and at home he prayed aloud so that his household would hear and learn how to pray. In [Jerusalem Talmud Peah 8:8:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Peah.8.8.9) it is related of him that when he saw a poor man of good family who had lost his property, he would say to him: “My son, I have heard that an inheritance has fallen to you — take a loan from me, and you will repay me.” And he expounded: “It is not written ‘Fortunate is he who gives to the poor,’ but ‘Fortunate is he who considers the poor’” (that a person must consider how to perform the mitzvah).[^16]
Hyman concludes from this that he was wealthy, and as we said above, his trade was in wine.
In [Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 8:1:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.8.1.5): when Rabbi Yonah drank four cups on the night of Passover, his head hurt him until the festival.

He was expert in the nature of animals, as in [Shabbat 155b:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.155b.11), where he expounded at the gate of the Patriarch’s house: “The Holy One, blessed be He, knows that the dog’s food is scanty; therefore its food stays in its bowels three days.” He merited a son, a great man of the generation, known as Rabbi Mana or Mani, who learned Torah from his father. Hyman points to Mani’s references to “Rabbi Yonah my father,” including [Demai, beginning of chapter 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Demai.4.1.6) and [Sheviit 4:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.4.2.5).[^14]

In Moed Katan, end of chapter 1, he asked Rabbi Yonah his father; in [Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:10:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Megillah.4.10.5), “When Rabbi Mana taught in the group, [he reported] teachings he had heard from his father,” etc.; and in [Nedarim 9b:8-9](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.9b.8-9), Rabbi Mani challenges it and Rabbi Yonah answers him.
Rabbi Yonah died before his colleague Rabbi Yose, as stated explicitly in [Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni 4:6:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Maaser_Sheni.4.6.4).
We find Rabbi Chanina, the brother of Rabbi Mana, as in Moed Katan 3:5, folio 13b; Hyman suggests that possibly he too was Rabbi Yonah’s son.

notes.text: The entire supplied Hebrew, all68 current/proposed English units and all current/historical notes were read. Hyman owns the generations, teachers/colleagues, post-Ami academy reconstruction and possible filiation of Chanina brother of Mana. His always/assertion/possibility force is preserved, without canonical identity or chronology admission. The initial והנערץ is visible and unresolved rather than silently changed to merited; supplied Berakhotיה./AZיה./BerRפט״ד־יב/Berפ״גכה״א remain literal instead of automatic number guesses. Source Challah7:1 stays visible and held; the tractate has no chapter7, but this does not authorize a guessed replacement. Rabbi Ami’s two list entries remain separate exactly as supplied. למחוייהאפיה in p007/p044 means paying a visit, not rebuking, confirmed by the whole saved Guggenheimer JTMeg4:5 paragraph2; Yirmeyah objects in a Torah-reading discussion, not prevents a rebuke. The actual saved Challah1:1 paragraph21 supports a challenge before Yirmeyah. Eight returned evidence scalars were fully read and hash/selector/meta bound. In p042 ר״ח remains a siglum: Chiyya/Chaggai alternatives survive in the note; saved DavidsonMK25a paragraph19 alone names RavChagga but is insufficient to prove the burial referent. p055 similarly retains fatherר״ח instead of an unverified Chiyya expansion; supplemental GuggenheimerYev2:4 returned a nonmatching section, not absence elsewhere. Supplemental Taan4:3 paragraph1 does have ElazarbarMerom objecting before Yonah; supplemental Meg1:1 paragraph10 has PhilippabarPeruta speaking before Yonah, so generic spoke replaces an asserted objection. Source name/location forms stay unchanged. Supplemental Sheviit5:1 did not match the YudanbarPalai phrase, and Meg4:6 did not match the Mana phrase; preserve those observations without global absence claims. The p066 כד הוה מרי בחבורתא phrase remains literal/held, not invented master-in-the-group status. Saved DavidsonNedarim9b paragraphs7–8 explicitly have Mani challenge and Yonah answer, so no question mark on that locator. The supplied headache endpoint עדהחג remains until the festival; saved GugShab8:1 has untilShavuot as a distinct reading. The prior reviewer Zevachim105a nonmatch remains a claim needing further evidence, not a root-proven absence; p061 held. RavHuna/RavChisda expansions in the rain story follow full named DavidsonTaan23b, without global title harmonization. All meaningful old notes/sourcequestions preserved. Digital editions are not printed pixels or correction-history proof.

Orlah’s supplied פ״ג סה״א specifies chapter3, end of halakhah1. In the synagogue-visit narrative, Yonah’s question is addressed to Yosah/Yose, who answers by pointing to Yonah’s teacher Yirmeyah; the saved named paragraph explicitly supplies that direction. These English clarifications do not resolve the separate יה. folio readings or establish a new discipleship chronology.

The consulted Jerusalem Talmud Orlah 3:1 records Yonah’s question to Zeira and the ensuing displeasure. In Bekhorot 30a the consulted edition reads Zeira in both clauses, while Hyman distinguishes Zeiri in the first from Zeira in the second. The consulted Chullin 43b gives Yonah and Zeira without titles. Hyman’s reports about the printed variants and the supplied locators are retained as he gives them.

Hyman’s printed p. 694 reads זכה עוד לקבל, “still had the privilege of receiving,” where the supplied text has והנערץ לקבל. In the consulted Bekhorot 30a, both alternatives name Ze’ira. Hyman differentiates the names and gives his own account of when Yonah studied with Yochanan and his disciples. The Jerusalem Talmud Yoma passage gives Yonah’s correction about consultation and service, and leaves his interlocutor unnamed.

The printed lines and named passages support Berakhot 14a, Gittin 59a and Avodah Zarah 14a, where the supplied text has יה., כט., יה. The consulted Challah 3:5 transmits the teaching in Ze’ira’s name. The exact Rif, Ein Yaakov and Dikdukei Soferim print readings are reported by Hyman.
Printed p. 695 cites Bereshit Rabbah 48:12. The named passage gives Yonah in the name of Chama bar Chanina, speaking about the wilderness of Sin and the wilderness of Alush.

The printed and supplied Berakhot locator includes the unusual suffix כה״א. The parallel at Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 3:1 gives Yonah and Yose the Galilean in the name of Yasa bar Chanina in the discussion of asking a ruling before a bier.

The printed Challah chapter numeral appears to be six, and the supplied Hebrew gives seven. Challah has four chapters in the consulted division. At Jerusalem Talmud Challah 3:1, Yonah reports a discussion involving Shmuel of Cappadocia and an unnamed sage, with two positions about whether there was enough to remove from the mixture.

Hyman’s print uses ר״ח for the person he says was buried in Tiberias. In the consulted Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 1:2, Rabbi Chaggai begins and Yonah and Yose conclude. Moed Katan 25a says Rav Chagga brought Rav Huna into Rabbi Chiyya’s burial cave. The excerpt leaves Hyman’s abbreviated name open.

The supplied Hebrew has Yevamot 2:4 and abbreviates the father’s name ר״ח. The printed locator and Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 12:4 support the comparison here. The latter explicitly names Rabbi Yitzchak son of Rabbi Chiyya citing Rabbi Yonah.
The printed locator is Zevachim 107a, where Rava opens with כדרבי יונה, “in accordance with Rabbi Yonah.” The supplied scan-derived text has 105a and places אמר before “that Rava.”

Hyman’s print has Megillah 4:10 and מורי, “taught,” where the supplied Hebrew has 4:6 and מרי. The named Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 4:10 passage distinguishes what Mana heard from his father at home and in the academy, with different formulas for citing him. Hyman gives an abbreviated quotation.

[Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 1:2:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sanhedrin.1.2.11) names Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yose as the two who conclude. [Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 2:5:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Rosh_Hashanah.2.5.2) reads Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yasa. [Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 2:1:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Eruvin.2.1.9) reports a question asked by Rabbi Nasa, while [Jerusalem Talmud Bava Metzia 3:1:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Bava_Metzia.3.1.2) has Rabbi Nasa citing Rabbi Yonah. [Seder HaDorot 1861](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=1861&lang=en) identifies this Rabbi Yonah as the father of Rabbi Mani.

In [Demai 4:1:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Demai.4.1.6), Rabbi Mana says that the rabbis’ words support Rabbi Yonah, his father. In [Sheviit 4:2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.4.2.5), he says he raised a difficulty before his father.

The Bekhorot discussion continues into [Bekhorot 30b:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.30b.1). [Berakhot 14a:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.14a.15) and [Berakhot 14a:18](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.14a.18) have Yonah transmit different teachings in Rabbi Zeira’s name. [Avodah Zarah 14a:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.14a.6) gives two versions, one ending with Rabbi Zeira and one continuing from him to Rav Zevid. The question and Rabbi Zeira’s displeasure are explicit at [Jerusalem Talmud Orlah 3:1:16](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Orlah.3.1.16). Hyman reports the reading at Megillah 15b from the Rif and Ein Yaakov.

In [Jerusalem Talmud Peah 8:8:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Peah.8.8.9), Yonah calls the money a gift after the recipient has accepted what he understood to be a loan. [Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 3:5:19](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.5.19) puts Yonah’s remark to Gurion in a discussion of mourning customs. [Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 8:1:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.8.1.5) says that the headache lasted until Shavuot.
